marine-iguana.relatives: The marine iguana's closest relatives are the Galápagos land iguanas, which live on the islands' dry interiors and eat cactus. The two lineages probably split around 4.5 million years ago or more, possibly before the present islands even existed, on older islands that have since sunk beneath the sea. Both groups descend from iguana ancestors that are thought to have drifted from South or Central America on rafts of vegetation. On South Plaza Island, marine and land iguanas occasionally interbreed, producing rare hybrids. Iguanas belong to the family Iguanidae, which includes the green iguana of Central and South America and the Fijian iguanas, which may have rafted even farther across the Pacific. Several marine iguana subspecies are recognised, each specific to a group of islands.

european-hedgehog.relatives: There are around 17 species of hedgehog, found in Europe, Africa and Asia; none are native to the Americas or Australia. The European hedgehog's closest relatives include the northern white-breasted hedgehog of eastern Europe and the Amur hedgehog of China and Korea. The four-toed hedgehog of Africa is the species most often kept as a pet. Hedgehogs are related to gymnures, or moonrats, of Southeast Asia, hedgehog relatives without spines, and more distantly to shrews and moles. Porcupines and echidnas also have spines but are not related; spines evolved separately in each group. Hedgehogs are an old lineage, with fossils dating back tens of millions of years, and their basic body plan has changed little.

komodo-dragon.relatives: The Komodo dragon is a monitor lizard, genus Varanus, a group of around 80 species found in Africa, Asia and Australia, which includes the Nile monitor and the lace monitor. Its closest relative is the lace monitor of Australia. Fossils show that the Komodo dragon's ancestors evolved in Australia, where a giant relative, Varanus priscus, also called Megalania, reached perhaps 5 to 7 metres long before dying out tens of thousands of years ago. Komodo dragons are thought to have spread west to Indonesia from Australia. Monitors are related to snakes, and they share the forked tongue and venom glands, part of a larger group of venomous reptiles.

peacock-mantis-shrimp.relatives: Mantis shrimp form their own order, Stomatopoda, with around 450 species, and are only distantly related to true shrimp, crabs and lobsters. They are divided into two broad types: 'smashers', like the peacock mantis shrimp, which club hard-shelled prey, and 'spearers', which have spiny claws to impale soft fish and shrimp. The spearers include some large species that ambush prey from burrows in the sand. Stomatopods are ancient; their ancestors appear in the fossil record about 400 million years ago, and modern mantis shrimp forms evolved by the time of the dinosaurs. The peacock mantis shrimp's spectacular colours and complex eyes are shared, in different forms, across the order.

common-eastern-firefly.relatives: Fireflies are beetles in the family Lampyridae, which has more than 2,000 species worldwide, including about 170 in North America. Not all fireflies flash: some fly by day and communicate with scent instead, and in some species the adults glow steadily rather than flashing. The firefly's genus, Photinus, includes many North American species, each with its own flash pattern, like a language. Predatory Photuris fireflies, nicknamed 'femme fatales', can mimic the female flashes of Photinus to lure males and eat them, gaining protective chemicals in the process. Glowworms in Europe and click beetles in the tropics also produce light, and bioluminescence evolved separately in several beetle groups.

ruby-throated-hummingbird.relatives: Hummingbirds, family Trochilidae, are found only in the Americas, with more than 360 species, most in the tropics of South America. The ruby-throat's closest relative is the black-chinned hummingbird of western North America, which looks similar but has a violet band on the throat. Hummingbirds are closely related to swifts, which are also expert fliers with tiny feet. Surprisingly, the oldest hummingbird-like fossils come from Europe, around 30 million years ago, suggesting the group once lived in the Old World before dying out there. The smallest bird in the world, the bee hummingbird of Cuba, weighs under 2 grams, while the largest, the giant hummingbird of the Andes, weighs about 20 grams.

wandering-albatross.relatives: There are about 22 albatross species, grouped with petrels, shearwaters and storm-petrels as 'tubenoses', seabirds with tube-shaped nostrils and an excellent sense of smell. The wandering albatross belongs to the great albatrosses, genus Diomedea, along with the royal albatrosses and several close relatives that were once considered part of the same species, such as the Tristan, Antipodean and Amsterdam albatrosses. The Amsterdam albatross, found on a single island in the Indian Ocean, is one of the rarest birds in the world. Some authorities now call it the snowy albatross when those close relatives are treated as separate species. Albatross fossils show that the family once lived in the North Atlantic too, including Bermuda, before disappearing from that ocean.
